analysis.one_liner: Replaces the income tax with a flat 20% tax on paychecks and business income, and repeals the estate tax.
analysis.headline: The bill had zero cosponsors and never left the Senate Finance Committee before the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would scrap the current income tax and replace it with a single 20% tax on wages, salaries, and professional fees, plus a 20% tax on active business income. Money from investments — capital gains, dividends, interest — would no longer be taxed as individual income, and the estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes would be repealed outright. It would also end the public financing system for presidential campaigns and repeal the financing mechanism for retired coal miners' health benefits.
analysis.who_benefits: People whose income comes from investments rather than paychecks: the bill taxes only 'earned income' (wages, salaries, professional fees) [S3], so capital gains, dividends, and interest would be entirely untaxed at the individual level [S3]. Estates and gift-givers gain from the full repeal of the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes [S3]. Coal operators gain from repeal of the coal industry health benefits subtitle that finances retired miners' care [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners living off investments and large estates

how_it_helps.text: The bill taxes individuals at a flat 20% of earned income after a standard deduction ($12,500 single, $25,000 joint, $6,250 per dependent), a capped charitable deduction, and home mortgage interest, replacing the bracketed rate structure [S3].

Businesses would pay 20% on active business income after deducting inputs, wages, and equipment, and the bill explicitly disallows deductions for lobbying and political expenditures, making lobbying more expensive for business [S3].
Supporters of flat taxes argue the single rate and simplified base make filing dramatically easier; the bill would repeal most of the current individual tax provisions in one stroke [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Wage earners bear the flat 20% rate on their paychecks while investment income escapes tax; the bill's structure would also eliminate the credits and deductions in the current system — such as the earned income tax credit, child tax credit, and state and local tax deductions — that sit in the subchapter it replaces [S3]. Retired coal miners would lose the dedicated financing for their health benefits [S3], and presidential candidates would lose public campaign funds, pushing fundraising back toward large private donors [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Middle-income wage earners and retired coal miners

drawbacks.text: A flat 20% tax on wages with no progressive rates and no low-income or child credits would raise taxes on many middle- and lower-income working families relative to current law, which has lower brackets and an earned income tax credit [S3].

Because only earned income is taxed, a person living entirely on capital gains, dividends, or interest would owe no individual income tax, while the repeal of the estate tax removes the only federal tax on very large inherited wealth [S3].

The bill repeals the financing of presidential election campaigns and the coal industry health benefits provisions without replacing either, ending a public campaign funding stream and the dedicated funding for retired miners' health care [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The genuine appeal is simplicity: one rate, one form, few deductions. But the design concentrates the benefits on people whose money comes from investments and inheritances — their income is exempt and the estate tax disappears — while the entire burden of the new 20% rate falls on wages, with the progressive rate structure, the earned income tax credit, the child tax credit, and most itemized deductions swept away. The quiet repeals of presidential public financing and coal miners' health benefits have nothing to do with tax simplification. As written, this is a large transfer of tax burden from wealth to work.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 2007 with not a single cosponsor and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Arlen Specter (R-PA) introduced the Flat Tax Act of 2007 on April 10, 2007 [S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day, and no further action was ever taken on it [S5].
The 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, and the bill died in committee without a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, wage earners kept the progressive income tax with its credits and deductions, large estates remained subject to the estate tax, retired coal miners kept their benefits financing, and presidential candidates kept public campaign funds. Nobody's taxes changed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wage earners and retired coal miners

for.name: Sen. Arlen Specter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Flat Tax Act of 2007 and delivered introductory remarks.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance (Chair: Sen. Max Baucus)
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: There is no vote record to measure: a single Republican senator introduced it, nobody cosponsored it, and it never came to a vote.

industries.note: The bill exempts investment income — capital gains, dividends, interest — from individual tax entirely and repeals the estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes. The tax burden shifts onto wages, so the gain for wealth comes directly at the cost of people who work for a living.

Repealing the coal industry health benefits subtitle would end the financing stream — funded by the coal industry — that pays health benefits for retired miners, relieving coal companies of the cost while leaving retirees without it.

The bill bars businesses from deducting lobbying, campaign, and public-influence expenditures as a cost of doing business, raising the after-tax price of influencing government. This is the one provision in the bill that works against money in politics.
Repealing the presidential election campaign financing provisions ends public matching funds, pushing candidates to rely on large private donations instead.
